title: Saladin's Trap at Hattin
text:
In the summer of 1187 Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, invaded the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem with a large army. King Guy of Lusignan gathered nearly all the kingdom's fighting men at the springs of Sephoria, a strong position with plenty of water. Saladin wanted a battle on his own terms, so he attacked the town of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee, where the wife of Count Raymond of Tripoli was besieged in the citadel.

At the council of war, according to the Frankish chroniclers, Raymond advised Guy to stay where he was, even though his own wife was at risk: the summer heat and lack of water on the road to Tiberias would ruin the army. Other barons, led by the Master of the Templars, Gerard of Ridefort, accused Raymond of cowardice and treachery. Guy changed his mind and ordered the march.

On 3 July the army set out across the dry plateau in burning heat. Saladin's horse archers harassed it constantly, and it failed to reach water. That night the Franks camped without water near the twin hill called the Horns of Hattin. Saladin's men set the dry grass on fire, sending smoke over the camp. On 4 July the parched army broke apart. Guy was captured and the relic of the True Cross was lost. Within months Saladin had taken most of the kingdom, and Jerusalem surrendered in October.
lesson: Do not let an opponent choose the ground for you. Pressure to look brave can push a leader into the very move his adversary planned.
people: Saladin, Guy of Lusignan, Raymond III of Tripoli, Gerard of Ridefort
source: Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani; Ibn al-Athir, The Complete History; the Old French Continuation of William of Tyre
